utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Oric, good morning to you. Could you tell me whether you could receive interpretation in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I am receiving interpretation and I understand the proceedings fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution together with co-counsel Ms. Patricia Sellers, and our case manager, Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I am Vasvija Vidovic, together with Mr. John Jones. I appear on behalf of Mr. Naser Oric. Joining us here today are our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries? I see none. Usher, please. As I said, I'll try to brave it throughout this sitting, but if at any given moment I cannot continue, then we have agreed that we'll apply Rule 15 and Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser will continue in my absence, with Judge Brydensholt presiding. But in the meantime I'll try and brave it. It's not the first time, and it will not be the last time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to repeat the solemn declaration. It continues to apply throughout your testimony. Ms. Sellers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, learned friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, yesterday you testified to a document that was submitted; it was Prosecution Exhibit 279E, I believe, and you testified that Srebrenica was one of the territorial places in which the 2nd Corps -- I would just like to ask you one final question about that document. In your expert opinion, would you say that any of the armed conflict or hostilities that occurred over the larger territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, those that occurred in Srebrenica were part of one and the same armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to turn to what will be my next-to-last area of questioning. I will keep to the time limit that I explained to Your Honours yesterday. Dr. Gow, I would like you to be precise as possible in explaining whether the Bosnian Serb forces, in your expert opinion, acted as agents, or were otherwise controlled by political forces within the Republic of Serbia or otherwise. I would like you to give specific examples as possible as to why you think, if you do, that the Bosnian Serb forces were controlled by such political entities in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's certainly my view that the Bosnian Serb forces were part of one integrated military/political framework, that they were, as far as they were separate from the Belgrade command and control arrangements, acting as proxies of Belgrade in that situation. And it was a case where, distinct from others, where perhaps an outside agent gives some form of support. Maybe financial, maybe arranging for facilitation of support. In this case, there were direct links, there was direct involvement at times. Your Honour, the Presiding Judge Agius yesterday asked the question about the command and control arrangements, I think, and then I was trying to indicate that while the Bosnian Serb military commander was given broad operational authority -- maybe I should explain the level strategic. You have political command, strategic level, which is the interaction/integration of the political and the military, and below that you have operational which is then the conduct of the armed force operations in pursuit of the political objectives, if that makes it clear. And within that context, the VRS commander was given, in my view, broad operational authority to conduct military part of the campaign without necessarily reference to the political level, but at times, there was still reference to the command level above in Belgrade, with the Chief of Staff, General Perisic, and both Mladic and Perisic were not only reported to be in communication with each other and meet each other at times, but also with the Serbian president, Slobodan Milosevic. Now, in that set of command-control arrangements, which is, at the least, you could say, was a dotted line, and that dotted line, as I think I tried to indicate through the Jovic diary entry was deliberately arranged in order to try to disguise the political control, the command and control arrangements for pursuing this objective, but it was an agenda set by Belgrade, it was an agenda fostered by Belgrade, and was not one in which Belgrade simply, on occasion, out of sympathy, gave some little bits of support. In concrete terms, not only were those arrangements in place so that the forces were effectively part of one armed force but under a different name. It's also the case -- and within that, I should say that a large number of those in the officer corps of the VRS continued to have the new -- old JNA and their new VJ passbooks. They continued to be regarded as part of the same command-control structure for promotion and pension purposes, yet they were seen as being part of one whole operation. And that in that context, and despite that arrangement to try to disguise the corps of political design and political command and control and military command and control, there were still occasions where it was judged to be necessary to introduce forces from the VJ, that is, those supposedly of Serbia and Montenegro, supposedly separate from those of the VRS. So you get the introduction of the 63rd Airborne Brigade in operations around Sarajevo in 1992 and 1993, special forces from Nis and Uzice involved in operations several times in Eastern Bosnia, particularly in Gorazde in 1994, the support from Montenegro and from those same forces for operations. Again in 1994, in southern Bosnia, at one point something like 4.000 troops are brought in across the Drina from Serbia to bolster the Posavina Corridor, in fact probably on two occasions one in 1993 and one in 1994. At the time of the initial international attention to Srebrenica in 1993, there was clear engagement of the VJ, both firing artillery from across the other side of the Drina and sending some forces over the river to be part of those operations. And there were VJ elements present in the initial parts, running up to the eventual taking over of Srebrenica in 1995. So there's a pattern, and there are other examples we could go to as well. The 9th Novi Sad Corps was involved both at Zvornik and Bijeljina later further down at Vlasenica. Cases you can point to throughout, where even despite this attempt to try and persuade the world that Belgrade was not responsible, because the world, in some sense, was regarding Belgrade as responsible, and that it -- the UN Security Council had imposed sanctions against Serbia and Montenegro because of this situation and because of its -- the perception in the Security Council that Belgrade was responsible for this action. So despite the attempt to pretend that that was not the case, to have this proxy force and say no, it's not us, really, it's them, it was always part of one operation, one whole integrated armed force. And despite the attempt to disguise, sometimes they even had to take the step of sending forces that were labelled as being from the neighbouring country and not being part of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would also like you now to respond to the following question: Was the Republika Srpska ever recognised as an independent country by the international community?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Republika Srpska has never been recognised as having independent international personality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: From the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina's point of view during the time period of the armed conflict, were they fighting an aggression for -- to stop the territorial disintegration of the territory that they constitutionally considered Bosnia-Hercegovina?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was their position. While the Bosnian government was clearly also taking a position to protect, as far as it could, the position of Slav Muslims within Bosnia-Herzegovina, given the situation, its formal position and its overall position was to maintain the territorial integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which, I might add, was also the formal position of the international community expressed through the UN Security Council resolutions and through the actions which were get -- to which those gave rise, such as in the introduction of the peace force in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So was the Republika Srpska a non-recognised political state which I'll refer to as an entity, was that the aggressor on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina from at least the point of view of Bosnia-Herzegovina for its territorial integrity?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think if you refer to the declaration of war, or the declaration of a state of war, to which we made reference yesterday, you'll see that the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina regarded various outside-Belgrade elements as the aggressor. But within that also included what they described in the document as the SDS terrorists. The SDS terrorists, using the term they use, without any other connotations to be attached to it, were the ones implementing the political part of the strategy to separate parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina from Bosnia and Herzegovina to become part of the Serbian construct that I described yesterday. So in that sense, they clearly regarded Belgrade, Serbia -- Belgrade, Serbia and Montenegro, as the aggressor and the armed forces of Belgrade, and saw the actors within -- from the Serb community within Bosnia-Herzegovina as agents of that action.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. I would now like to turn to Prosecution exhibit document, the next document in the binder before you. Dr. Gow, did there come a time period when the armed conflict or the armed hostilities, as you described, came to an end, an end that was recognised by the international community?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: The phase --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can go direct if you want here. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or just lead the witness, and he will then finish it off.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, are you familiar with the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was the purpose of the Dayton Accords to formally end the hostilities that we've described that occurred between 1991 and 1995 when the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. I would draw your attention to the document. I would ask you to please look at the -- may I, for the record, just put the ERN of the document in. That would be 03631869. Dr. Gow, I'd ask you to look at the second page of that document that ends in number 70. All right. The first paragraph, which starts with the "The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina," would that be an accurate representation of who or what states were considered parties to the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. There we have Croatia, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and Bosnia. I would now like to draw your attention to the fifth paragraph down with begins with "Noting." Dr. Gow, you see in that paragraph that the Republika Srpska is not -- having not been included in the first paragraph as one of the parties, there is an explanation. Could you please give the Trial Chamber your opinion, or does this - excuse me - substantiate your opinion as to one of the reasons that the Republika Srpska might not have been considered an independently recognised state?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that it's one of the explanations, but it's a confirmation that Republika Srpska was not recognised as having independent international personality. And in that context, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was the agent of international personality signing the agreement. If I can go back, we should probably be clear that the parties to the treaty, although that was designated at the beginning, that they are also parties to the conflict is a distinction we should probably make clear. And you could also add within that that the Croatian forces, and Croatian political movement and Republika Srpska were also, in some sense, agents to the party. Agents -- parties to the conflict within that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I thank you for that clarification. I would now like you to look at Article 1 on that page, and I think that if we could just ask for your commentary on the part that has been highlighted in yellow. Now, this refers to the territorial integrity and political independence of Bosnia. Is that consistent with the explanation that you just gave the Trial Chamber on one of the aspects of this armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It confirms that the parties to the conflict, in the end, despite the intention of one of the parties to the conflict at least, have agreed to respect and maintain the territorial integrity and political independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is supported by the international community.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now ask you to go to Article 2, the first sentence in Article 2. And you would agree that there are certain military aspects to this settlement that would be further highlighted in an annex 1A of this document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now ask you to go to the page that has ER number 73 on the end. I believe it's about two pages over. Looking at the top of the page, Dr. Gow, would you please inform the Trial Chamber of the date in which the armed conflict, according to the document, ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: This general framework for peace agreement was signed on the 21st of November, 1995, in Paris, and it was signed, as you can see, by the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, the president of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, and the president of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic, on behalf of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And I think we should also probably take it as significant in the context of the discussions we've had about the nature of the armed conflict and political authority and command and control on the Serbian side, that it was the president of Serbia, not the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, who was the party to the treaty signing on behalf of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When did the armed conflict officially cease, according to international instruments?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this international document.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly ceased on the 21st of November, 1995, in terms of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I would ask you now to go to the following page that ends in ERN 74. And do you agree that attached to this document were several annexes, that annex 1A, that we referred to earlier, would look at specific aspects of the military -- military aspects of the peace and settlement?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now ask you to go to the page that ends in 76 and the ERN number, approximately two pages over, at the bottom of that page, is Article 2. Your thoughts about the cessation of hostilities. Dr. Gow, there's a reference to another date there. That's the date of October 5th 1955. Would you please explain to the Trial Chamber the importance of that date.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was initially an agreement to cease-fire as a prelude to going to the Wright-Patterson air force base in the United States to conduct the negotiations for the general framework of peace agreement that eventually was concluded, although I would point out that despite the cessation of hostilities agreement, some armed hostilities continued after that period on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Would you please turn the page over, and the first half of the first paragraph, Dr. Gow, would you agree that forces within the meaning of this document then included armed civilian groups, national guards, army reserves, military police, the Ministry of Internal Affairs' special police force?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right. And would they be considered the forces that we have been discussing throughout your testimony?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask you to go to page number -- that ends in ER - I'm sorry - 78. It's just, I believe, one page over. Article 3. Dr. Gow, I would draw your attention to the first two paragraphs, and in paragraph 1, would you agree, or would it be your opinion also, that there were foreign forces that were on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina during this time period of armed conflict? Is that consistent with your prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. And if you would look at paragraph 2, would you agree that some of the foreign forces would include advisors or trainers or volunteers, personnel from neighbouring and other states, freedom fighters?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. And so would you also agree, that is, with the cessation of hostilities, that these other actors were covered by this agreement so that the armed conflict could completely cease?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Sellers and Dr. Gow. Let's make this clear. The fact that this is stated in this international document, or this document, does not prove that the situation was identical at any time or throughout the entire conflict. It only means that at the time this document was signed, this was considered to be the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But this doesn't prove that in 1992, the situation was identical.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree. I would just state that this seems to be the understandings of the parties at the time that they are signing the document. I don't think we can go much further than that. And that takes me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- my last page of this document that ends in ERN number and number --

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before you move on, may I add something on this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also with reference to Your Honour's comment. That I think we should also to some extent, if not entirely, see the Security Council Resolution 752 from May the 18th, 1992, almost as one end of the parenthesis and this is the other end of the parenthesis, both of which in some way regard that external involvement in Bosnia and Herzegovina as part of this. I should also point out two things for clarification. In the second paragraph there, reference to foreign forces is not only those of the Republic of Croatia and Serbia -- Serbia and Montenegro, but of course so-called freedom fighters, because there were those that came from other parts of the world and, in some cases, came to join an international brigade as part of the Bosnia and Herzegovina defence forces. And the other is that, I think if we look at paragraph 1, is just to explain the reference where it says, "whether or not they were legally and militarily subordinated to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." This is a clear reference to the fact that some of the armed forces, namely, those of the VRS, were subordinated not to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina but to the external agent.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: May I just have a question to this article. Could you perhaps focus a little bit on paragraph 1. You would see the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina or Republika Srpska. Now, here is Republika Srpska put on the same level. Is this different from the -- what was it, from the original agreement or ...

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was a doubt in Your Honour's mind, I'm glad -- I'm very glad you asked it so we can clarify. The reference here is to the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina or Republika Srpska. Under the term -- de facto at the point of making this agreement, and under the terms of the agreement, if you will - maybe in your own time to go and read annex 4 which embraces the constitution that comes into place under this - Bosnia-Herzegovina is to comprise two entities, the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is internationalised, with a Z, and the Republika Srpska. So these are the two entities within Bosnia and Hercegovina, with a C, the country. So where there's reference to Republika Srpska here, it's as one of the two entities, the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is the -- you get preceding that immediately. You get -- it is the reference there. Both of those are referring not to the country but to the two entities within it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers kindly slow down for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could I ask you now to go to the page that ends in ER number 93. It's several pages over, and it's a signatory page. Page 25 of the document. Dr. Gow, I believe this is a signatory page to annex 1A. And would you agree, is it your expert opinion, that the signatories to this annex 1 represent here different signatories than we've had for the first part of our document? And is there any explanation as to why the Republika Srpska signs at this point?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two additional signatures, those of representatives of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and of the Republika Srpska, the two entities to which I just made reference within Bosnia-Herzegovina. There are two explanations for that. One goes back to the same explanation I gave with reference to your first question on this document, and that is the initial parties to the treaty were not necessarily the parties to the conflict, although they were also parties to the conflict. This is making clear that even within that, whatever claims there are to be -- to the divided character within Bosnia and Herzegovina, because it's quite clear that the conflict was hybrid -- had a hybrid character, both international and non-international, that the non-international parties to the conflict also signed the agreement. So you have a Jadranka Prlic, the prime minister of the federation of Bosnia-Hercegovina and Momcilo Krajisnik, the president of the Republika Srpska, signing on behalf of the authorities, as well as having Izetbegovic, Tudjman, and Milosevic signing on behalf of the three states.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask the registrar, could I please have a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be P416.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document is being admitted in evidence as a Prosecution Exhibit P416.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. That allows me to move to the last area of my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I would ask you to inform the Trial Chamber, did you write a report in regard to the testimony that you gave today, and give it to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. And I believe it might be the last document in your book. I would just like to confirm that you then signed that report on the 5th of September, 2004.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what it says on the end, I'm sure it's true. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And in that report contains your curriculum vitae, which has a list of the different publications that you have written in addition to your other professional activities.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has a selection of those things. It has some publications and it has a small bit of things that I've done.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And is --

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can provide you with a much fuller one if you had the time to be bored with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And your testimony also has been based upon many of the subject matters that you have raised in this report.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has, although we've extended beyond the scope of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask that Dr. Gow's report be submitted into evidence, if I could, and I would ask the registrar, could I have a P number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be P417.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask to tender Dr. Gow's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document is being admitted in evidence as Prosecution Exhibit P417, together with its annexes and everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will conclude my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sellers. Who will be cross-examining? Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Gow. I will mainly ask you those sets of questions to which you will preferably provide short answers. But whenever you believe there should be further clarification on any of the questions, please do elaborate. Likewise, sometimes I will have to touch upon subjects that you elaborated on yesterday during your testimony. This only means that we believe some further clarifications are required. In your testimony yesterday, you talked about the Serbian project, of a new state. This project, did it imply that all Serbs should live in the same states, meaning both Serbs from Croatia and Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was often a slogan that all Serbs should live in one state. Of course, while they had the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the other versions of Yugoslavia before that, that was the case. So this is not simply a matter that all Serbs should live in one state, but it's a matter of creating a new state of territorial boundaries, with a new demographic disposition within it that we're talking about. Not simply whether all Serbs should live in one state, assuming that those Serbs wished to live in that state.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would that mean, then, that territories being taken away from Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina were being annexed to Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the intention of the project, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were non-Serbs living in these areas, Croatian Catholics and Bosnian Muslims, weren't they? What did this mean for them specifically?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be clear, what did the project mean for them?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the way I described yesterday, using the strategy of ethnic cleansing, it meant that, for the most part, they were obliged one way or another, either through death or physical evacuation, to move.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow, for this clarification. A brief question now about the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Sciences. In your previous research, probably you have looked into this issue. Can you just please tell the Trial Chamber what the principal ideas are contained in that memorandum.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: The memorandum which was prepared by the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts in, I think it was, 1998 was questioning the constitutional position of Serbia within the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. In particularly, there were concerns that the two autonomous provinces within Serbia compromised Serbia's sovereignty; i.e., Serbia could not have the full exercise of sovereign rights over a designated territory of the state of Serbia. That this meant that its position within the overall federal construct was weakened, and that as a result of this, it was felt that Serbia had, in some sense, and I'm certainly paraphrasing here, become a victim of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, and that something would need to be done to change the position, to reassert sovereignty and to reassert the position of Serbia within the Yugoslav construct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that this memorandum was an ideological basis for what later unfolded throughout the territories of the former SFRY, or at least in part?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if you would be right. I know that there are many people who say that that's the case. I would hesitate to say it myself. It was certainly an important document, an activity in the process of changing the atmosphere and politics in Serbia, both reflecting some of the pressures and, later, being a dynamo for them. Whether or not you can say it's an ideological template, I would hesitate to say, but I know that other people do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can we please just have a correction in the transcript. The transcript reflects 1998 as the date of the memorandum, whereas you said -- yes, 1988, indeed.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said 1988 but, a personal slip. It should be 1988, sorry, yes. 1998, a very different document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. Do you agree that, following Tito's death, there was an explosion of nationalism?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately following Tito's death, it's remarkable that there wasn't an explosion of nationalism, given the expectations that many people had about Yugoslavia. But also it's quite clearly the case that levels of nationalist pressure that were contained within Tito's communist Yugoslavia, without Tito's influence, began to grow. And in the kinds of discussions that I summarised yesterday, the arguments about the future of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, what you could describe as nationalist politics was a dominant feature. So -- I'll just add. So that affected the dynamic, again, through the 1980s and to the point where Yugoslavia comes to break up.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. You wrote an article in July 1994 titled "Serbian Nationalism, A Hisssssing Ssssnake in International Order: Whose Sovereignty? Which Nation?" I will not ask you anything specific about this article. Everyone has access to it. But what, to your mind, does the slogan mean, "only togetherness will save the Serbs"?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what I'm supposed to answer to that question. Am I supposed to go beyond what literally does it mean, or am I supposed to give some sense of further explanation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you can be more specific. As I take it, as I understand it, is you're being referred to an article that you wrote in which, supposedly, you have also stated that "only togetherness will save the Serbs." I think that is what you're being directed at.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I understand what I'm being directed at. Literally, it's usually translated as only -- "samo sloga Srbina spasava", it's usually translated as "only unity will save the Serbs." Talking to people, I suspect that something like harmony is maybe a better translation of it. But the implication, unless I'm trying to get at: Is it simply what does it mean or is it the further implication. It's used as the four Ss of traditional Serbian symbols around the cross -- in Serbian, these are Ss -- and it's used to indicate that many of the Serbs believe there's great disunity within the Serbian community, whatever that is, within Serbian populations, that they are in some way threatened. This goes back to the Fourteenth century history, and that only by pulling together will the Serbs be able to protect and defend themselves. So that unity, or harmony idea, only if the Serbs agree and then together will they be able to protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed, Dr. Gow. The question I wanted to ask was: Does this point to the essence of the idea that Serbs are only safe if they live in one state, their own state?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be one reading of it. It's not necessarily the original sense of it, and it doesn't necessarily imply that Serbs living in one ethnically homogeneous state is for that to be the case. But it would be one reading of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that fear was fermented among Serbs and that this sphere was exploited by the Serbian National Party, the so-called Serbian Democratic Party, which I will in future refer to as the SDS. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, of course.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's certainly reported to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the SDS in Bosnia-Herzegovina followed the idea of the project of creating a new state? Did it display any separatist tendencies in relation to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and yes, it did. And I think part of my testimony yesterday went to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, is it not true that their intention was to separate part of the Bosnia-Herzegovina territory by force and annex it to Serbia Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it not true that, in order to achieve this, both military and political preparations were carried out, both in Yugoslavia and among Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, that is the case, and I think again, my testimony yesterday went to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let us first try to tackle the political preparations step by step. Whenever you think necessary, please do elaborate, if there's any issue that you believe needs further clarification. Yesterday you explained that in October 1991, a decision was made on the setting up of an assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Dr. Gow, there was a legally elected assembly of the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so this would have constituted a parallel organ of government, would it not?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, if I may correct you, I didn't testify to that yesterday. I don't believe that I mentioned it. But I would acknowledge that that took place. And I would also acknowledge that it was a parallel -- a parallel structure being set up outside the normal framework.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, throughout 1991, after establishing an Assembly of the Serbian People, they went on to create other parallel structures of government; is that not true?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, and I did testify to that yesterday; and also that they began to set up some other structures prior to October as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: By setting up these parallel bodies of government, they displayed clearly their desire to fully separate, entirely separate, the Serbian people from the other peoples living in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the intention was to separate these territories covered from the rest of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony, you explained that the SDS leaders, through the assembly, proclaimed the establishment of the autonomous provinces in Bosnia and Herzegovina in November 1991, the provinces that we usually refer to as SAO, S-A-O?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Although the last of them was in January '92, Birac.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did say that too, that two more provinces were eventually established. Is it not true that the Birac SAO was also at that time, which includes the Bratunac and Srebrenica area --

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Was in January 1992. That's not in -- sorry, I was just being clear when you said 1991 that Birac was in January 1992. But, yeah, it is true that Birac was established as a certain autonomous province.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance now, please. I would like to show the witness a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I will now show you a transcript of the meeting of the Bratunac SDS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I ask if we're likely to need this again?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please look at these minutes of the Bratunac SDS meeting held on the 25th of October, 1991. Can you please look at item 4. In the English version, it should be on a page 9. There is a total of 119 pages, and this is on page 9. Can you please have a look. I'm quoting: "The committee accepts the decision on the establishment of the Birac SAO." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says on the document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, does this confirm that the Bratunac municipality, in fact, accepted the establishment of the Birac SAO, as you've told us previously?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you repeat the question, please? Did you say the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that the Bratunac SDS accepted the establishment of the Birac SAO?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think originally you said the opstina, but it's the SDS committee, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly indicates that they recognised that that's happened, although I think, if I may add, paragraph 3 above it -- this handwritten document, I'm not sure anything else about it, but taking it at face value is also about the crisis staff in the Bratunac municipality, as I said yesterday about this process of preparing for takeover.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence, and may it please be assigned a number as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be D61.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document is being tendered and admitted in evidence and marked as Defence Exhibit D61. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, in your testimony, you stated that the Assembly of the Serbian Peoples, on the 28th of February, 1992, adopted a decision to proclaim the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina describing the Serbian state as the state of the Serbian people and other peoples. You also said that the constitution was eventually amended, and that the Republika Srpska virtually identified itself as a state of the Serbian people. What would that have implied for non-Serbs in this sort of parastate?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a possibility that you could make argument that -- to say it was a would-be state of the Serb people, but that would still leave space for other people to be citizens. But it is significant that the reference to "other citizens" is removed. And I think that by the time the Republika Srpska constitution was promulgated at the end of 1992, to some extent, it's also a reflection of the de facto reality on the ground, which is that the overwhelming majority of the non-Serb population as being one way or another removed from that territory and is laying claim to a purely ethnonational of it, ethnonational definition of it, or ethnocultural. I said "ethnonational." Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can I just add another question. This constitution, can it be considered as one of the foundations on which the policy of ethnic cleansing of non-Serbs from the area was later based, namely, from those areas that the Serbs, for one reason or another, considered their own?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand the question, I'm not certain you can say that it's a base for it, but it's certainly part of that programme of activity, and it's consistent with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. On the 12th of May, 1992, the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted a decision on the strategic objectives of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did it not?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm prepared to take your word for the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will now show you the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance, please. I would like to show Dr. Gow, the Chamber, and the Prosecutor this document, the decision on the strategic objectives of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina, adopted on the 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, can you please pay close attention to the strategic objectives number 1 and number 3. Can you please tell us whether it is true that the strategic objective number 1 is about the territorial separation from the two remaining ethnic communities. You can read it for yourself. You can look at both of these objectives, and the strategic objective number 3 about the setting up a corridor in the Drina river valley, or, rather, about eliminating the Drina river as a border between the two Serbian states. Also, can you please tell the Chamber, in relation to this, please explain: What did this mean for non-Serbs living in the Drina river valley and other border areas of east Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I can confirm that the document in front of us says the things that you said. The second thing is that, indeed, intention to have control of the western side of the Drina, as part of the overall project that we've been discussing now over these past two days, implied the removal of non-Serb or non-loyal, in case anybody decided they wanted to be part of -- stay there in these situations, population. If I could add, if it's not indulgent, if I could add a third thing, which would be ideally with reference to a map. But there was the intention to occupy this territory and also to form another corridor along the river Klivaj, between Olovo running up towards Tuzla. I've forgotten the name of the town at the top end of it, which would then be part of encircling Tuzla to make broad corridor across the whole of the northern top. So when this makes reference to a corridor -- makes reference to the established corridor between Semberija and Krajina, that can refer to the now Pasavia corridor, which is already there, but I think it's also implicit that it's meaning to, if possible, to establish this broader corridor. The reality was that Serbian forces were never strong enough to be able to complete that. But they did occupy the western side of the Drina to take control of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Can this exhibit please be assigned a number as a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be D62.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document is being admitted in evidence and marked as Defence Exhibit D62.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The first strategic objective indicated in this document spoke about the drawing up of state borders, separating them from the remaining two ethnic communities, those two being Muslims and Croats; is that not true?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that at the time in east Bosnia, there were mainly Muslims, that they were the predominant ethnic community, in addition to the Serbs living there, of course.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say, off the top of my head, I couldn't say whether or not that was accurate in terms of numbers. I'd make reference to the map we have here, which shows that certainly it was a very mixed area, with large numbers of Muslims in the population, but also significant -- some significant Serbian populations. I mean, my recollection would be that it was predominantly Muslim. But without specific information, either in my head or to hand, I'd say that. But there were significant number of Muslims in that region, I think would be the main point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, do you have at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, if you have at your disposal a demographic map that you can refer the witness to, I would suggest you do that, as that will economise on time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At this moment, I don't have a map with me, but I have another map that will assist us as we go on. May I ask you, Dr. Gow, to look at this map of this particular part of Eastern Bosnia made up by the National Bureau of Statistics of the Republic of Croatia as a study of the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina. May the map also be placed on the ELMO, please. Dr. Gow, I will kindly ask you to look at the map and maybe also use the pointer there. Could you point to us at the river Drina on this map. It's merely an excerpt from this larger scale map that you used yesterday. Could you please point at the river Drina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I am having a problem. Although I see that the document has been placed on the ELMO, I don't think that the ELMO is switched on, or at least I am not seeing anything on the video mode. No, no, no. Oh, I see, I see. So you have to go on the video mode, the first button, in order to be able to follow. No, no, no, it's gone now. But it will come again. But that's where you have to be. Yes. Dr. Gow, sorry for having interrupted you like this. You were asked if you could be kind enough at the river Drina on the map -- on the map. That's all.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'll see the Drina is marked there. The Drina more or less runs consistently, the border between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia, so the outside edge of this map as it runs down, almost all points is the river Drina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Gow, I would like to refer you back to the strategic objective number 3 from the document we mentioned earlier on, and in relation to this map. This objective said that the Drina should be erased as a state border. Would that mean that the territory around the Drina river should be annexed to Serbia? Was that the plan, to annex that area to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plan was to annex that area to Serbia, or to create a border between Serbia and the Republika Srpska, whatever this new construction was going to be. But as I recall -- I don't have the document at hand anymore, but as I recall, it didn't say that that was the intention, to erase the border. That was just the implication of what it said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, just to help you, the translation that I have of the third strategic goal of the 12th of May is to "establish a corridor in the river Drina valley, that is, to abolish the Drina as a border between the Serbian states."

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the first part of it, or the second. That's fine. Then in that case, then, absolutely, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Do you agree that this particular region is known as the Drina valley or, as they call it Podrinje?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that the plan was for the entire region to become a part of Serbia, the entire region of Podrinje. That's what we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: To become part of the new state, whatever the new state would be called.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Of the new state. Very well. Thank you, Dr. Gow. Could you please point to us the town of Zvornik on the Drina river, on this particular map. Can you perhaps circle it in some way, circle the town, and then place your initials.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you use the highlighter, please.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be clear, you wish me to mark on this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you also mark the town of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Next, please mark the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that these towns are near the Drina river and the border with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you also please mark two more towns in this part of Eastern Bosnia, namely, Vlasenica. I will ask you some matters concerning its importance later on.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And Han Pijesak, that you mentioned yesterday, and I believe you can see it here.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, yesterday you said that the town of Han Pijesak was, throughout the war, the main headquarters of the Serbian army, was it not?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that -- not even so much that. But in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, this was where the main operational headquarters for wartime was located, and that this remained part of and, indeed, as I understand it, remains to this day part of an integrated operational command-control setup, yes. And so therefore it was a vital, as a command and control point, in the war, and as a point in integration.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, it is true that in this small town in Bosnia, there was the headquarters of the Serbian army during the war, and that significant military forces were stationed there.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That it was -- that it was the command-control point, and "significant" in the sense that command and control is significant and important, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Can you tell me what's the distance between this particular point and the towns of Srebrenica and Bratunac, if you know?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but it's a few kilometres, 10, 15. I don't know exactly. I don't know what the scale of the map is. It's not very far.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Dr. Gow, let us now turn to the context of the military preparations that followed for a war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Yesterday you said that the armed forces of the SFRY consisted of two elements, the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence, and that the Yugoslav People's Army was reorganised in order to prepare for the war. Is it true that, during 1991, the process of the Serb dominance in the JNA dramatically shot up? Within a very short period of time, the 40 per cent of Serbs in the JNA went up to some 90 per cent; is that true?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, that somewhere between the summer of 1991 and March 1992, the proportion had become about 90 per cent, and of the other 10 per cent, you take into account Montenegrins and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You also said that this process was accompanied by the withdrawal of the JNA units, their equipment, and weapons, the MTS, that is, the materiel and technical equipment, from Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: You also said Slovenia. The translation didn't. Was I correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Slovenia and from the non-Serbian-controlled parts of Croatia, that's true, that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout 1991, there were organisational changes made to the Yugoslav People's Army where the second military district was formed in Sarajevo. Is it true that the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was thereby covered by two military districts, namely the mentioned military district in Sarajevo and the fourth military district in Titograd?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection was also that the fifth military district from Zagreb covered northwestern Bosnia. But without going back to check any of that, I would affirm those three things with caution.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Right. It is true that the second military district was, indeed, established in Sarajevo; is it not true?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Going back to what I said yesterday, also, that the 2nd military district was then converted into the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. Is it not true that, as part of this process and of the strategy of the Serbian JNA, the policy of assuming control over the communication centres was also something that took place?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And again, my testimony yesterday went to that point. Excuse me, could I just ask, are we going to be using this again, because I would rather move this away because it's quite difficult -- I'm kind of peering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you finished with that map, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We can move it back later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, in the meantime, perhaps you could move the ELMO back, because I understand the witness -- it's standing right in the -- I agree with you, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, I minded it as well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that, by doing so, by taking over control, the Serbs gained advantage, because the other side was left without these significant military resources? And I'm referring to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask for the answer to be entered in the transcript. He said yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shall repeat it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the takeovers include repeaters, other important facilities, as well as some issues, like the ones you mentioned yesterday, some important sections of roads? But could you please tell me, did this also include the takeover of repeaters and some other important facilities?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: It included the takeover of all facilities -- of all military means and materiel that were under the control of the VRS of the 2nd military district. There were some areas, such as Konjic, where there was fights over control of some of the assets. But in most places where the then-JNA, transformed -- about to be transformed into VRS, couldn't establish control, as with Slovenia and Macedonia and the non-Serbian-controlled parts of Croatia, the tendency was to raze things, to destroy, not to leave anything behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We will come to that later when talking about the context of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Could you confirm that the military and political leadership from Belgrade, through the reorganisation and transformation of the armed forces, in effect, weakened the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it not true that the entire weaponry was taken out of the control of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and placed under the control of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain it was the entire arsenal, but it was, by far and away, the overall majority of it. The Bosnian forces did keep -- were left with something, they had something as it started. But most of what they had was gone.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. Is it correct, is it true, that the weapons and materiel that had been taken over were then transferred to the areas predominantly populated by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were redistributed to Serbian Territorial Defence, Serbian-controlled Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly ask the usher to show the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are we finished with this then?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Could the map please be assigned a number. I've forgotten all about it. And could we tender that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be D63.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So the map on which the witness -- Dr. Gow, marked several places and put his initials next to the markings is being admitted into evidence and marked as Defence Exhibit D63.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness please look at the document by the Federal Secretariat For National Defence of the General Staff of the armed forces of Yugoslavia in Belgrade, addressed to the commander or chief of staff, that is, by -- to the second military district, signed by Lieutenant General Ljubomir Simonovic. It says it is a note from the meeting of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence regarding the situation in the second district in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and a proposal to pull -- to relocate units of the JNA and the VMR. This is a note of the meeting of the secretaries for National Defence concerning the second military district in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the proposal to relocate the JNA units and the VMR. The document is a long one. Please look at item number 1, and then we'll look at item number 4. I can quote item number 1. The note orders that: "As soon as possible, staffs should be established, detachments and brigades of volunteers of smaller numbers, and that they be reinforced by officers of the JNA with weapons and equipment." Could you please look at item number 4. It says: "To plan and secure mobilisation call-ups in the areas predominantly populated by the Serbs, whereas in the other levels, a high level of combat-readiness should be ensured for the JNA units." Dr. Gow, I believe that in your studies you had occasion to see this document. Does this, in fact, not mean that the JNA has started forming volunteer units? And is it not true that the JNA did, in fact, establish volunteer units?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was actually hoping -- going to ask if I could make a comment on the document. But as you say --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: By all means, doctor.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you say, I might have seen this document in my studies, I would say I haven't seen this document. And I'm prepared for the discussion now, to talk about it and take it at face value. I would raise a question about it, if I may, which is simply that the typeface is -- it's consistent with my understanding of situation and events, but the typeface is different than any other I have seen of documents, which means that it looks different and inconsistent, and therefore I just raise that question about it. I have no way of verifying its provenance and authenticity. I don't want to raise questions about it. I'm prepared to take it, and it's consistently my understanding, but it doesn't look like other documents from the JNA, especially because of the -- the typeface is very different. But given your questions, and that I take it on that basis at face value, certainly it's consistent with my understanding, and it certainly indicates military preparations underway. It would refer to the action for coordination with war -- opstina, municipality, war presidencies, crisis headquarters, and local security services to be working in conjunction with the JNA and in the process of mobilising Territorial Defence to prepare the armed forces there. I might also add that paragraph 5, you made reference to Han Pijesak before, I made reference to it yesterday, indicates clearly, if the document is being taken at face value, that the preparations to relocate the second military district headquarters from Sarajevo to Han Pijesak for the wartime command and control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we break, perhaps -- there seems to be the signature on this document, what purports to be the signature of Dragoljub Simonovic. Have you ever seen the signature of this person before in your life, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Have I seen the signature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Have you seen the signature of Dragoljub Simonovic.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I have. I don't have a specific recollection of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have the break now, if it's convenient for you. In the meantime, do you want to have a further look at this document during the break, Dr. Gow, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It can do no harm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I could make it available, and then we'll reconvene in 25 minutes from now. That's basically ten -- between ten and five to 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Apologies to my learned friend. I just wanted to return to the Trial Chamber the inquiry that was made. We asked that two Prosecution exhibits be tendered. They were tendered. They were tendered only in English. We now have the B/C/S translation for those exhibits. And that's Exhibit 410 and Exhibit 411. I wanted to place that on the record and have these handed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They are already in the record because you have just stated it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we don't need to do anything more about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Those were the two documents that were tendered yesterday, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Madam Vidovic, you may proceed. In the meantime, if the witness, having gone through -- having had the opportunity to go through this document once more, would like to add anything else to what he stated before, before answering any further questions, you're free to do so. Otherwise, you can wait for the question and answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I, just before the witness answers, provide a clarification. The witness is actually right. This is not a document of the JNA, this is a document of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. This is something that the witness, I believe, should bear in mind for any further clarifications, should he deem that any are necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Are there further comments, either from the witness -- you may remain silent on it, if you refer to do so, or any further questions, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, it would probably be better to remain silent. I just wanted to confirm that what I was -- what I was intending to do before was simply to indicate that I have -- I would have a question about the document. I don't want to dispute the document as such. But just because either from Federal Defence Ministry or JNA, it looks different to other documents I've seen in terms of the typeface. I haven't -- I can't say for sure even that I haven't seen another document that has a similar typeface. But just it looked unfamiliar. Certainly, the information within it is consistent with my understanding of what was happening, and it could well be that -- you know, it can be taken that it's not for me to decide what the document is. But I wanted to raise that question simply to say that I look at it and I think that probably the -- in assisting the Trial Chamber, the Trial Chamber might want to be aware that it looks different to other things. I could also suggest that in pursuing this, in handwriting on the original, it says "Annex Expert Drina Corps." I don't know where the document came from, but that might also help, if anybody does want to pursue it at a later stage. And also, while I have the document, and taking it again at face value, would add also, consistent with both some of the things I said yesterday and with response to some of Madam Vidovic's questions, and I hope I'm not preempting Madam Vidovic in saying this, I should also point out a couple of other things. The first is that if you look under -- I think it's Article 2, item 2, and you go to the third indentation -- sorry, I've got the original. This is on page 3 of the translation. Both that and the following indentation confirm about destroying and disabling all equipment that cannot be transferred to Serbian control. There was another thing which is -- oh, and I understand why Madam Vidovic was asking about the 2nd and 4th military districts, because under the JNA I also mentioned the 5th covering northwestern Bosnia, but by the you come to this document, of course, the 5th is no longer functioning. So now I understand why you asked that before. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, do you have any further questions on this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. No further questions in relation to this document. Just another clarification. It may happen in other cases too, to the Trial Chamber and the Prosecutor. Sometimes we receive documents bearing certain markings, documents that we receive directly from a source. This document is from the seized documents in the 2nd military district in Sarajevo. The source then hands this document over to us, and the document bears a mark. There is nothing I can do about this sign or mark. Thank you very much, Your Honours. I would like to tender this document into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P64.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: D. This document is being tendered in evidence and is being admitted and marked as Defence Exhibit D64. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to this, we'll no longer be requiring this document. You've elaborated on this sufficiently. Just one question. The destruction of military structures in this way, did it affect the military ability of the Bosnian army at a later stage in terms of the equipment that it had? Later, at the beginning of the war, and throughout 1992.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course it did. It meant that materiel which might have -- if left behind untouched, could have been available to the Bosnian army. Sorry, materiel that could have been available to the Bosnian army was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you, Dr. Gow. Now I will show you a different document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show Dr. Gow, the Chamber, and the Prosecutor a document of the Serbian Assembly of Foca municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it, Madam, that you no longer require these two documents? No?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are OTP translations, if I may. These are not Defence documents. But my eyesight is not what it used to be, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see, I see, I see. So these -- can you indicate to me which is 410 and which is 411?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P410, and this is P411. Okay, thank you. Sorry about that, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I hope that Dr. Gow, by now, has received this document of the Serbian Assembly of Foca municipality, a document that was sent to the JNA general staff in Belgrade personally to General Colonel Blagoje Adzic. The title is "A Request for Stationing in Foca," dated the 17th of March, 1992. Can you please look at the very last sentence of the first section or paragraph of this document. It reads: "The building is some 2 kilometres away from the town, and it is located in an area populated by Serbs only."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have translation? [Interpretation] Does the Chamber have this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then if you could please look at the following paragraph of this document, which says: "Pursuant to our request, we have made some previous arrangements and submitted the necessary documentation to the Bilaca Corps HQ. You can now make all the necessary consultations in this regard with the above-mentioned corps HQ." Dr. Gow, Foca is a town in east Bosnia, is it not?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it not true that there was a degree of close cooperation between the SDS and the JNA in terms of these preparations that were carried out? Does this document not demonstrate that this was, indeed, the case?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, again, consistent with things that I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have the usher's assistance yet again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just why we have -- one other thing about the previous document that I intended to say. This is addressed personally to General Colonel Blagoje Adzic who was referred to in the previous document. Just for clarity on the record, the translation said that he was a representative of the Defence Ministry. He was actually acting defence minister, which is reflected in the original, just so it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.
