utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document please be assigned a number as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be D65 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document is being tendered -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I know it's going to be tendered. I just want to ask learned counsel would she please just clarify the origin of this document. I see that on the top it says "Institute For War Crimes." Is this the origin of the document that we're looking at just now, or does it come from a collection? We note it has no ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is that the Dutch Institute for War Crimes?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was about to shed some light on this. This is the institute for researching war crimes, an archive with documents that were seized from the 2nd military district based in Sarajevo. This is a document that the Prosecutor has already used in a number of other cases, if that can be of any assistance. I, however, obtained my copy directly from the institute.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. We'd have no objection therefore, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So this document is being tendered and entered in evidence as Defence Exhibit D65. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I asked Dr. Gow to look at this document, a document of the Serbian Assembly of Foca municipality, a document that was sent to the General Staff of the JNA in Belgrade. Actually, we finished with that. But now I want him to look at the Serbian Assembly of Ilidza document, dated the 3rd of January 1992, signed by Assembly President Radomir Kezunovic. There's a reference to it here as draft decision. If he can please look at item 1, item 1 reads: "Start an initiative to regulate the status of Serbian volunteers, members of their families and members of territorial units." Dr. Gow, in relation to this document, can you please explain the following: The cooperation between the SDS and the JNA, was it not material in terms of preparing volunteers, and did it not cut both ways? Do you not believe that that is precisely what this document shows?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly agree that it was important. I didn't catch the original, and the translation says "cuts both ways," and I'm not sure what is meant by that, just to be -- just -- just to clarify the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What I wish to ask is, was there a correspondence, mutual reporting, from the SDS to --

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And vice versa.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Gow, could you explain the meaning of this cooperation between the SDS and the JNA in terms of arming the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may be brief, I think I did that yesterday. But it was part of the military/political plans to pursue the project about which we've been talking.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And to a high degree, this project was being implemented by and through the SDS.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it wasn't explicit yesterday, let me draw it out and make it explicit. The SDS was pursuing the political dimension with the strategy in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in doing so, was relating to those preparing the military dimension.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I was about to ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document for the Serbian Assembly of Ilidza, dated the 3rd of January, 1992, be assigned a number as a Defence exhibit, and I would like to then tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be D66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document is being tendered and received in evidence and being marked as Defence Exhibit D66. One moment. My attention is being drawn, very rightly so, by Judge Eser, that this purports to be a draft decision. Do you have any information at all, Madam Vidovic, whether at any given point this -- what purports to be a draft eventually was adopted and became a decision? Do you have any information on that, or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Serbian municipality is here making a proposal to start an initiative on regulating the status of Serbian soldiers, which indeed was regulated at a later date, as will be clearly indicated by further documents that we are about to produce. What I wanted to speak about was that there was a degree of cooperation in terms of making proposals and decisions. That was my intention. I wanted to get our expert witness to explain what communication there was mutually between the SDS and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we are on the same wavelength here. Although this document says the Ilidza municipality at its first session on the 3rd of January, 1992, adopted the following," then it says "draft decision." Either it has been adopted, or this is a draft decision presented for adoption and this is the document which was presented for adoption, taking it for granted that it would be adopted on the 3rd of January. But what we'd like to know is whether it was, indeed, adopted, in which case it would have been followed by another document without the use of the word "draft." So, I don't know, I mean, this is not the first time I have seen documents like this. To be honest, in Brdjanin, we had hundreds of such documents, and most of the time you never know whether they became decisions or whether they remained as drafts. Yes, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I hope this helps. To situate in context, I made reference to an instruction from the SDS leadership yesterday which was sent out in December to the local SDS parties to begin these kinds of operations -- this kind of procedure. So I would situate this is part of a process begun in December. The date of this in early January seems to me to indicate they are taking part of an initiative. And whilst we can assume nothing, I would take it as read from later events that this process was continued and completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do you have anything to add, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just this: What we have here is a situation where different bodies in the area were authorised to do different things. This is a low level of government making a proposal to a higher level of government to adopt this particular decision, which was adopted on this very day. The proposal to submit this to the assembly was adopted on that day. You can see that based on this decision. It says: "The decision is hereby being submitted to the Serbian Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina for further realisation." So as far as this particular body of government is concerned, the Assembly of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza, this is the final document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Can I have the usher's assistance, please. I would like to show the witness a different document. And the document is -- my apologies. Before we start with that, can we please have this document assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be D66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I had already said that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. But I seem to remember that I had already said that. It's okay. No problem. It's D66 anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, can you please have a look on the conclusions based on the assessment of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the area of responsibility of the 2nd military district, dated March 1992, signed by Commander General Milutin Kukanjac. Can you please look at page 5 of the B/C/S version, which should be page 6 of the English. Page 6 of the English, the section which reads: "The JNA has distributed 51.900 pieces of weapons (75 per cent), and the SDS, 72.298 pieces." Dr. Gow, does this document not confirm what you spoke about yesterday, namely, that there was a very high degree of cooperation between the SDS and the JNA in arming the local Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does. And if I may add, with reference to that earlier document yet again, that made reference to the report from the 2nd military district command, and from the date, I would assume that this is -- taking the other document at face value, this is the report to which it makes reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Dr. Gow, does this document not indicate that the JNA was, in fact, receiving accurate information from the SDS as to the exact amount of weapons that had been delivered and distributed by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Plausibly it could do that. It could also indicate the number -- the pieces of weaponry which the JNA had given to the SDS to distribute, without necessarily confirming whether or not and how they had been distributed. But I think that would make a big difference to the point you wish to address.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Therefore, the JNA and the SDS were obviously distributing tens of thousands of weapons to the Serbian population while they were carrying out preparations for the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you explained that an important role in implementing the policies of the Serbian leadership was played by paramilitary formations set up by security services in Serbia itself. Is it not true that there were special camps back in Serbia used for the training of these units?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's certainly true that there was at least one camp, yes, and that they were coordinated at the air force base at Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does a camp of Arkan's units in Erdut mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the one camp to which I made reference when I said there was at least one camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Were people who were trained in this way being sent to Bosnia-Herzegovina to fight there, at the beginning of the war? And later as well, throughout 1992.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, paramilitary units were, in fact, involved in taking control of Srebrenica, expelling its population, looting property, torching houses, and killing Muslims in the first half of April 1992. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned Srebrenica. The translation did not say Srebrenica. You have to be cautious about having tactical knowledge about the level at Srebrenica. I have information from some places. I wouldn't commit to any specific statement on Srebrenica, but that was happening generally throughout parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including those regions in Eastern Bosnia. It's certainly the case. And that paramilitary were playing a central -- a key role in that process.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I forgot a moment ago about this document, a conclusion based on the assessment of the situation. May that document please be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, D67.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document is being tendered and accepted in evidence and marked as Defence Exhibit D67. Ms. Sellers, it also doesn't show provenance, or this doesn't have an ERN number. Like the previous document, it says "Institute For War Crimes." Maybe at this stage, Madam Vidovic, you can give us the information as regards provenance, even though the Prosecution hasn't objected.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour for raising it. I'm just going with the policy of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We received this document from the institute for researching war crimes, the Bosnia-Herzegovina Institute. It was taken from the archives of the 2nd military district in Sarajevo where documents were seized. Likewise, this is a document that has been used by the Prosecutor in other cases here. However, it was much simpler for me to simply obtain it back in Sarajevo from the institute. I hope that is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you say "seized," seized by whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following the withdrawal of the 2nd military district that used to be based in Sarajevo, the documents were left behind and were seized by the police forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, police and military forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's clear, not to give the impression that they may have been seized by some officer of the Prosecution. All right. So that's D67, I repeat. Madam Vidovic, you may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the usher's assistance now to place the document by the military post of Zvornik or, rather, that it be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document by the military post of Zvornik, dated 13th October of 1992, entitled "From the Commands of the Soldiers from Zvornik Brigade to the Birac Brigade." I will quote one part of the order, which says: "Temporarily dispatch the unit from the 6th Infantry Battalion, called Beli Orlovi, from our brigade to the Birac Brigade, to carry out combat assignments." Dr. Gow, Beli Orlovi, White Eagles, are known as the paramilitary unit of Vojislav Seselj from Serbia; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's certainly the case that there was a paramilitary organisation called Beli Orlovi that was organised by Vojislav Seselj, and it's possible that this makes reference to it. But I don't think we could entirely exclude the possibility that there was some other infantry battalion called Beli Orlovi, and that it might make reference to that as well. But certainly there was a paramilitary force called Beli Orlovi.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of the Beli Orlovi being active in the area of Eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, it was active in Eastern Bosnia. I have to say that I have -- I'm getting old and I don't remember things specifically. But I seem to recall introducing evidence to that effect 10 years ago, when I was assisting the Tribunal in a previous instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That doesn't help.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Telling us that you're old doesn't help us much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Forgive me, Your Honours. I wasn't meaning anything else.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Seselj's units were active, and as I recall in the specific evidence I introduced at that stage, we also had some videotape of Seselj saying directly that he discussed this with Slobodan Milosevic, and about how it would be deployed and used in places in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have a question in relation to this. Is it not true that, in fact, there was a high degree of coordination between the State Security Service in Belgrade and the local Serb military units with regard to the engagement of these units? I'm not referring here merely to Seselj's units but to paramilitary units in general.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: If by "local units" you mean the paramilitary units, and I don't see them as local because they're coming from outside, but if by that you mean the paramilitary units, then yes, they were -- they were planned -- they were initiated and/or planned and coordinated through the Serbian security service, through the control of General Frenki Simatovic within the command structure within the Ministry of the Interior and the security service in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is it not true that in the spring of 1992, the Serbs provoked different incidents and situations as a motive to break out with the conflicts between the Serbs and the rest?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's certainly my understanding in a number of areas. One part of the pattern of takeover was acts of provocation. I think I said yesterday that part of the pattern was having a particular place, town, village, surrounded with JNA units and artillery and armour. What very often would happen was also that within that community, there would be an incident which would be an act of provocation which would then lead to some -- a Serb, a group of Serbs within the place calling for assistance, at which point the operation would go into plan -- would go -- the plan would go into operation. Sorry, not the operation would go into plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I turn to my next question, could this document be assigned a number as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be D68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Registrar. This document is being tendered and admitted in evidence, being marked as Defence Exhibit D68.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, is it not true that the Serbian authorities established by the SDS had planned to take control over the municipalities where there were Serbs, regardless of whether they were majority or a minority?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, with the qualification that it was not necessarily all places where there were Serbs. But certainly places where the Serbs were not in a majority were part of the framework.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it not true that even some Serb municipalities were established that had not existed previously, namely, Skelani and Milici?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think any Serb municipalities existed prior to this process of beginning to declare places as Serbian municipalities. Before, they were simply municipalities. I don't know if that helps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does. Thank you. But were these municipalities, to your knowledge, in fact, established, namely, Milici and Skelani, which were not on a list of municipalities in the previous time, earlier on? If you know.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have -- not being an expert on local government in Bosnia, if those were new names, I wasn't aware of it. But I have seen the names Milici and Skelani. So if they didn't exist before, then I would presume that they have been established in the way you describe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I take it --

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not being an expert on the local government --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fair enough, Dr. Gow. In fact, when you see that it's beyond your territory, then tell us so. But I take it you mean to suggest to the witness, to Dr. Gow, that Milici and Skelani, supposedly before becoming Serbian municipalities, formed part of some other municipalities. But they were not municipalities on their own score. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's be more specific. Milici formed part of which municipality before becoming a Serbian municipality itself?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The municipality of Srebrenica, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Skelani?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the municipality of Vlasenica; I apologise. Skelani was part of the municipality of Srebrenica, whereas Milici, that town was part of the municipality of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then at a certain point in time, you maintain that they became Serbian municipality of Skelani, Serbian municipality of Milici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They therefore became separated and were turned into Serb municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have any knowledge about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Eser would like to add something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic, as I said, I still have some problems to understand what you mean with Serbian municipalities. Does it mean that these municipalities have been different before a certain point, and then that Serbian people would come?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's something historical to be explained. Let it come out. It will be explained.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the expert could help us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, taking also into consideration the point raised by Judge Eser, Judge Eser --

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's precisely what I wanted to make clear. It's possible, especially given some of the questions you asked yesterday about demographics and ethnicity, that we need to make a distinction between areas that might have been, in a casual sense, described as Serbian, because the majority within the municipality happened to be self-describing ethnic Serbs. And those which were part of a process which began in April of 1991 of -- by the SDS or local activists of describing the term of "Serbian opstina," Serbian municipality, to certain of the municipalities. And I'm taking it from the interchange between Judge Agius and Madam Vidovic now, that within that process, of which I wasn't aware, that part of this was also declaring certain parts of some existing municipalities also to have this label. So it's not about -- necessarily about the casual description of Serbian representing the population, but about this additional process of adding the label "Serbian" to the names of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Dr. Gow. I would now like to show you a document, which is the Defence Exhibit D30. This document is entitled "The Guidelines for Work," by President Radovan Karadzic, dated 15 August 1991, sent to the SDS municipal boards in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: "The Guidelines for the Work of the SDS."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to look at point 4,"Binding Guidelines for Work", which says: "Every member of the local board must be tasked with some 10 to 20 homes that he has to keep in contact with." In relation to this issue, Dr. Gow, my question is as follows: Is it not true that the SDS organised the Serbian/Bosnian population, including the lowest level, the grassroots, going as far as the Serbian homes? Does this document not point to this?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, including the lowest level, the grassroots, going as far as the Serbian homes? Does this document not point to this?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the benefit of the public that may be following the proceedings, can we have the English translation -- yes, probably, on the back side -- put on the ELMO as well. Please. Thank you. Yes, go ahead. Sorry to interrupt you like this, but usually we have it the other way around.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, just to clarify, I think it is clear that, although this is about the -- the document refers to the opstina, just to be made clear that items 3 and 4 are working -- are talking about local committees, so the organisation there is talking about at a neighbourhood level.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow, for your explanation. My question is the following one: Does it not mean that the entire Serbian people, or at least the better part of it that lived in the territory of Republika Srpska, were mobilised for the war, or at least was being prepared for the war?

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. "Prepared" is the better word. I'm not -- in the context, assuming that this document -- assuming certain things about this document, I think we can see that it's consistent with an explanation for the way in which there was a phenomena at the time of takeover operations, where very often, in the 24 to 48 hours preceding, many of the -- if not all the Serbian inhabitants of certain places would move out. Certainly large numbers. I don't know that this necessarily implies that. But the idea of this connection with local arrangements, people in neighbourhoods being responsible for communicating informally without documents verbally, with people in houses would be consistent with that. But it doesn't necessarily say that that's what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it not true that the SDS boards, in the beginning of the war, were, for the most part, transformed into crisis staffs.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that crisis headquarters were formed as part of the takeover process, yes. Whether that's necessarily to say that they're transformations of the -- of the SDS boards is not something to which I would be able to testify. But that the crisis headquarters were prepared and took over, and that, again, would be consistent seems to be reasonable, or seems to be a reasonable inference, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, could you please explain to the Trial Chamber the role of the Serbian crisis staffs, in brief, both in the preparatory stage and in the beginning of the war; in general, to state whatever you deem was significant concerning the crisis staffs in order for the entire issue to be understandable.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something, again, to which I made reference yesterday, but I think to be clear, crisis headquarters were part of the structures for preparing for takeover. The aim of the crisis headquarters, through the instructions, was to prepare to form a government to identify those who would be potential opponents or significant leadership figures to make sure that they were identified and detained or otherwise dealt with at an early stage, to ensure that there would be coordination with the security services and local police, to ensure there would be coordination with the JNA. As part of the -- that was the preparation. And in the implementation, the role was to execute those tasks and to make sure that, in a particular area, any potential opposition was removed or sidelined, that the new Serbian authority government, self-claiming, self-purported, was put in place to replace any existing municipal authority, and from that point, to begin political leadership in line with the programme that we've been discussing in that particular area. So that would include removing, would include further coordination, and, in that case, political direction to any elements of security forces at the coordination with the military.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak in the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Gow. Could you please look at the following document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the usher's assistance. Could you please place the document on the ELMO. This is a document by the MUP of the Serbian Republic -- the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Before we turn to the substance of the document, this document was obtained on the basis of a subpoena by the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this was on the request of the Defence, not the OTP. Therefore, the MUP of Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, 31st of March, 1992, signed by the assistant minister of the interior, Mr. Momcilo Mandic. It was addressed to all, as you can see in the heading, the CSBs, State Security Services, all, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the second line, which is pretty long. It says: "In addition to this, the assembly of the Serbian of the Serbian Republic adopted a number of laws and regulations necessary for the functioning of the Republic of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina." In this context, a law on the interior was passed, which would be -- be in application as of the 1st of April, 1992, in the territory of the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and appointed Mico Stanisic as the minister. Dr. Gow, in some of the statements that you made so far, at the request of the Tribunal, for instance, in your statement relating to Vlasenica of the 25th of October, 1994 [Realtime transcript read in error "2004"], you studied the role of the Serbian police. First of all, I will ask you the following: You are aware of the fact that the Serbian police was established, as this document indicates.

utterances.speaker: Andrew James William Gow [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, I see in the transcript the 25th of October, 2004. But I think you said 25th of October, 1994. Which one is the correct one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because the transcript says 2004. But I'm sure I heard you say 1994. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will be changed in the transcript. Thank you. Dr. Gow, please proceed.

By "Serbian police," if you mean police by the self-declared Republic -- Serbian Republic of -- Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then yes, if that's what we understand by Serbian police in this context.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what I mean. Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber the role that the Serb police had in the preparation of the and at the outset of the conflict.

Well, first of all, if I may, I'd expand it a little bit, because you're saying police, but the Ministry of the Interior was responsible for the police but, as designated here, Stanisic is being appointed as the Interior Minister. But it's pointing out also the role of the security service. So we're looking at two elements here. The MUP generally was given a role in setting up the institutions -- as one of the institutions of the newly declared political entities in setting up and taking part in the takeover, including designating and identifying those who would be potential opposition, and securing public order in their terms, which would also include meaning providing information and securing the detention of those people. They would also be involved with armed units, coordinating with military, with the JNA, as part of the armed forces operating on behalf of those pursuing the Serbian campaign.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you gave the statement on the 25th of October, 1994, you stated that a significant role in the preparation and the start of the conflict was played by the police in Vlasenica; is that correct?

I'm taking it that you have the statement in front of you and that I made that statement within it. By now, I have no recollection of the statement per se. But I don't have a question if that's what's there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fair enough. That's fair enough. Usually the practice is if you have the transcript, you show the -- or read out the relevant part of the transcript, and also indicate the part from the transcript to the Prosecution as well.
If I may add also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

-- if we're to discuss Vlasenica, going back to something I said before about local government. If I'd prepared -- in preparing a statement on Vlasenica, whatever I looked at at that time specifically relating to Vlasenica does not mean that I have specific expertise on Vlasenica and the situation there, and I necessarily recall any of what I might have looked at at that time. But if you have things and you wish to confirm that as far as -- and a whether you mean the same, I'm happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Dr. Gow. Do you believe that the police played a significant role -- I apologise. Do you believe that the police played a significant role in the very origins of the conflicts in central Bosnia, including Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I was a bit confused there.

Yes. The MUP was one of the elements of the security operations and was a key to it. It was one part of the formation in the process of taking over, as indeed, seeing as we discussed some other things yesterday, it would have been in the old Territorial Defence system under the general people's defence doctrine. I would expect and anticipated that the MUP and the JNA as well as the Territorial Defence forces would be integral parts of whatever operations there would be. So I think, yeah -- I think we can always take it as read that the MUP, in both its police and security service dimensions, would be part of -- a key part of whatever was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I turn to my next question, could, please, this document by the MUP of the Serbian Republic, of the 31st of March, '92, be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit, and assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be D69.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. This document is being tendered and admitted in evidence and marked as Defence Exhibit D69.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, before I move on to my next question about the war itself, I will ask you a series of questions on the role of propaganda in provoking the war. Is it not correct that the Bosnia-Herzegovina TV, the Sarajevo-based one, was not being received in Eastern Bosnia, that there was no reception of the Sarajevo-based programme? Or, rather, is it not true that people could watch TV Serbia only in Eastern Bosnia prior to the outbreak of hostilities?

I'd have to preface anything, again, with the caveat that this is beyond specific expertise. I am aware that it's generally said that people in Eastern Bosnia generally watched RTS. I'm also aware that at later stages, the broadcasting by RTS or by Serbian authorities, through special transmitters, was interrupted and blocked by NATO action, because -- in that context. But really, in terms of the -- you know, broadcasting ranges and rights, for what I can see here and now, I'm not certain that I'm the right person to be talking about it. But I'm happy to talk about it as far as I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Is it not correct, in as far as you know, is it not correct, then, that TV Belgrade kept broadcasting disquieting reports of an anti-Muslim character/nature in order to get the Serbs to stand up against the Muslim population?
In that summary form, something like that, again, is what's reported by the -- by those who've looked into these matters, and also perhaps even in the press as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically you don't have firsthand or even secondhand information, personal information about it. You're just relying on --

I have secondhand information in that I've read studies about these things over the years. I don't think it's particularly my place, my expertise, to be commenting on these things, although I know something about them and about the situation. But I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Dr. Gow, I will now show you an excerpt from a book which I will ask you to comment upon.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can have the usher's assistance, please, I wish to place on the ELMO afternoon an excerpt from Dragan Jovanovic's book, another author is Gordana Bundalo, and yet another, Milos Govedarica. The book is called "The Eradication of Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993." Can you please look at page 91 showing cuttings from the Serbian press at the outset of hostilities in 1992 and 1993. Can you please have a look at that page. I'll quote: "An unheard of massacring in Gorazde, bodies floating on the Drina, new testimonies, a Serb impaled, the river Sutjeska running blood, and hostages on a stake." Dr. Gow, in connection with what you told us yesterday and today, is it not correct that in Eastern Bosnia and Foca, mentioned here specifically, there were crimes that were perpetrated against the Muslim population and not against the Serbian population, as these newspaper cuttings seem to suggest.

It's true that there was extensive commission of actions that have been alleged to be, and, in Trial Chambers here, confirmed as crimes against Muslim communities -- Muslims in Muslim communities in Eastern Bosnia. I don't think that it necessarily follows from that that that means that there cannot be crimes against non-Muslims. It seems to me the logic there is crimes against one does not necessarily imply that there cannot be crimes against another. And just to be clear, I'm not sure if there's meant to be a direct connection between the previous two questions about the preparations and the broadcasting of RTS, and my comments about the press in the run-up to hostilities and the preparation and these two -- and these extracts here, because these are clearly from 19 -- post-1992/1993. So we're no longer talking -- just to be clear, if we all understand, we're no longer talking about the preparations, we're talking about events after the onset of armed hostilities. Just to make sure that that -- that we're clear and we understand that. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask technicians, we're not receiving any interpretation. The last portion, the B/C/S interpretation, the last portion, we have not received it, myself or Mr. Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But please, Dr. Gow, can you repeat your answer to my last question, simply because Mr. Oric failed to hear the interpretation. It is for his sake that I will now ask you to repeat your answer, if you can, if you would be so kind.
Gladly, as best I can. Should I see the transcript and repeat what I said or try to approximate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you have the transcript in front of you, you can actually read out from the transcript. In the meantime, I want to make sure that Mr. Oric is receiving interpretation of what I am saying, myself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I suppose you can go straight to the text that you have and read it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could we ask whoever controls this to go up a little bit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, you can't do that. I will do that, but I have to go -- I'm one page up. It's 67. So this is -- the question to you was as follows: "Q. Dr. Gow, in connection with what you told us yesterday and today, is it that in Eastern Bosnia and Foca, mentioned here specifically, there were crimes that were perpetrated against the Muslim population and not against the Serbian population, as these newspaper cuttings seem to suggest." And the following was your answer: "A. It's true that there was an extensive commission of actions that have been alleged to be, and in Trial Chambers here confirmed, as crimes against Muslim communities, Muslims in Muslim communities in Eastern Bosnia. I don't think that it necessarily follows from that that that means that there cannot be crimes against the Muslims. It seems to me the logic there is crimes against one does not necessarily imply that there cannot be crimes against the another. And just to be clear, I am not sure if there is meant to be a direct connection between the previous two questions about the preparations and the broadcasting of RTS, and my comments about the press in the run-up to hostilities and the preparation and these two -- and these extracts here, because these are clearly from 19 -- post-1992/1993, so we are no longer talking, just to be clear, we're no longer talking about the preparations, we're talking about the events after the onset of the armed hostilities. Just to make sure that we're clear and we understand that. Is that clear?" And then we were stopped because we had this problem with the interpretation. Mr. Oric, have you now been able to follow completely the answer given by the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, are these examples of inflammatory Serb propaganda designed to show that Serbs were, in fact, the victims, and designed in order to perpetuate the crimes against the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would say that calls for speculation in an area of expertise that Dr. Gow has tried to caution the Trial Chamber is not specifically his. I'm certain that he could speculate and answer, but I did want to reflect that I think we've already reached a bit of the limits in terms of his expertise as it relates to propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. Perhaps you can rephrase the question, basically, Madam Vidovic. I don't know whether it is needed or not. Because these -- at least what we have here is part of a book. That is what it is. The book is not written in defence of the Muslims, it's written in defence of the Serbs. And this is the eradication of the Serbs in Bosnia. So, I mean, the two go together, but there is no other way of explaining it. Yes, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm aware of this book, and I'm aware that it was part of a concerted propaganda act by the Serb -- by Serbian authorities, including from Belgrade. Indeed, I was given a copy of this book directly by a member of the Serbian Diplomatic Service as part of the efforts to draw awareness to this issue. Knowledge of the specifics of the television, broadcasting and press activities in Bosnia is not something that I have as a kind of primary concern. I do have primary interests in issues of propaganda and media. And one thing I would always want to get clear is that propaganda is simply about using information for your own purposes. It's not necessarily either untruthful or invented. It might be selective in its use of the truth. It might colour things in certain ways. But one of the things always to be clear about is that propaganda is simply about the use of information and the dissemination of information for a purpose, and it's the intent that makes it the propaganda. And in that context, the fact that this book was produced in response to alleged atrocities against Serbs in eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina, I think, is simply that the Serbs was trying to maximise whatever there in this context, and getting somebody from the Belgrade embassy in London to give me a copy of that and others was a part of that activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Eser?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, could you give us the year of the publication of this book, and could you give us the dates of these subtitles, the newspapers? At what time was this newspaper report -- did appear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's start with Madam Vidovic first. I suppose the year of publication, you can easily give us? Yes, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This book was published in early 1994. I will come back to the Chamber with the exact date. As for the newspaper articles, I really cannot say. I simply made a photocopy of exactly as much as was published was in the book itself, and the book did not contain any date in relation to these cuttings. The reference, however, is to events at the very beginning of the war, and that's as much as I can conclude based on the substance of these articles. However, if Your Honour so wishes, I may as well move on now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Are you satisfied with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Are you tendering this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document is being tendered and admitted in evidence and marked as Defence Exhibit D70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sure that the Defence will bring all the dates, but if I can point out that the one -- the one item that's marked "Sutjeska Teka Kerovovo" [phoen] is from Novosti on Saturday, the 12th of September. The year is missing, but because of the references to JNA and UNPROFOR, I suggest that that probably has to be September 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that. It actually shows the print there as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will certainly check this, and I will submit to the Chamber the exact date of publication of this book. I do for a fact that this was in 1994. Maybe it was late in 1994. I do have to keep my reservations concerning the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, what I gather from your answer to my last question a moment ago is that you were interested in propaganda as a field of study, and media, too. What I will now show you is a report by Renaud De La Brosse, a report submitted to this Tribunal. I will merely read a handful of excerpts and ask you to comment on those specifically just to see if you agree with certain portions of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have this report given to the witness. We have as many copies as we need to distribute to all the parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, could you please look at page 93 of this report. I will now read to you 93. It is the last sentence of paragraph 110. I will read it out to you. It reads: "Questioned by the RTS on the reasons which had led her to volunteer to fight at Vukovar, a young Serbian woman in uniform, mother of two children, said, 'Well, when I watch television, I see what's going on and I want to help. And I understood that it was worth sacrificing my life for our Serbia.'" Is it true, or do you agree, that the Serb-based Belgrade media were used in this way in order to get as many volunteers as possible to volunteer for military service in order to be sent to Croatia, and later to Bosnia-Herzegovina, to take part in combat?

First of all, I'm grateful to you for helping me in my research by bringing the specifics of this to light. I think -- was this report prepared for the Milosevic trial? I think I've seen reference to it there, although --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.
-- I haven't seen the report itself.

I think -- I can confirm that this is what it says on the page here. If I'm going to go beyond the page, I'd have to go to research that I've been involved in now, not relating to the case of the former Yugoslavia, but I'm actually in the process of part of a research project which, since 1991, has been looking at the media and use of the media in the context of current conflicts. And I'd have to say one thing from the research there, and I'm sorry if this is not very helpful, but generally it's helpful, and that is that there's no necessary way of saying how people will receive a message. Quite clearly those putting out messages have intentions in hope that the messages will be received in certain ways. But audiences tend to receive in different ways. If you have a predisposition to receive a piece of information, you will tend to react to it affirmatively; and if you have a predisposition against a piece of information, or an item, you will tend to react against it, people will tend to react against it. And in that context, I don't think we can draw -- we certainly cannot draw any necessary and linear connection between the transmission of a piece of information, or transmission of a television report or something in the press, and the way in which it will be received, because it will be received differently by different people, probably according to their predisposition in the first place. So in that context, I look at this and I would say I think it's very likely that the Serbian woman identified here, in taking this, would probably also have had a predisposition already to receive that information in a certain way, while somebody else, perhaps a Muslim from Bosnia-Herzegovina or from Sandzak in Serbia, or even a Serb who was not thinking in the same ways within Serbia, would react -- they might react differently. So I think we have to be very cautious in trying to draw inferences in linear connections between transmission and reception, and that's an area where I think I can speak with a limited degree of authority, because I have been working specifically on those areas in the context of the current so-called war on terror. Again, I confirm that I don't have that specific expertise relating to broadcasting, and so forth, in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then I will try asking you a simpler question in this regard. Is it true that in media reports, the Muslims were always referred to as Turks, Croats as Ustashas, and the Muslims, again, as Mujahedin? Was it not being suggested all the time to the Serbian people that they were the victims of attacks by non-Serbs, thereby underestimating the real danger posed at the time by these self-same Serbs to the other ethnic communities?

It's certainly the case that -- I don't think we can say always, but we can say that fairly consistently the Serbian news media, and indeed probably some cultural media, in the phase of the run-up to the war -- to the onset of armed hostilities, and continuing beyond that, certainly used language in the press, such as Ustasha, referring to Croatians, the implication being that -- to make a link with the fascist Croatian regime in the Second World War and therefore Serbs were being threatened in the same way. And I say that without any implications for whether or not the Serbs were being threatened, but simply to say that was the intent in the Serbian printing. And similarly the constant references to Turks, which you'll also see coming up in cultural reflections in films such as "Lepa Sela Lepo Gore." I can't be towards -- it's a way of expressing and dealing with these things, with historic references and the implication that historic references being both that people might tend to do that, but also to have implications to try and draw on forms of historical memory. But those references, a part of the cultural pattern, I think, but also was going to be -- depend on the disposition of people in the first place of how they're going to react to it. Whether they're going to say, you know, that's wrong, or whether they're going to say, yes, that fits with what I think already. In that context, I can confirm that that language was being used. So I think the evidence from some of the research, for example, by Mark Thompson on the press indicates that probably the reception of it within the relevant communities, because propaganda is usually aimed at a particular community, and in that case, it was that -- the Serb community that was receptive, so it would be taken in that way. I should also point out the same study also indicated the ways in which Croatian press, Bosnian press, and others also shaped information and agenda to their interests as well. It's a normal thing to do in a conflict situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you very much, Dr. Gow, for this elucidation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move on to further questions, can this report please be assigned a number as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know whether the Prosecution wishes to take a position on this. But this would be trying to admit in evidence an expert report in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I do acknowledge the Rules of Evidence that you set forth at the beginning of this trial, and that we tend to admit more than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But this is something different, Ms. Sellers. This is admitting into evidence an expert report taken from another -- from another case, without bringing and making available the person who drew up this report, and without presenting him as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: But, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if anything --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- in addition to that, I would like to raise the point that I believe our expert has not necessarily rejected, nor assumed the correctness of this report. So I would just add, in addition to -- I think it's not the best evidence because it's not the best witness, that now our witness really has no relationship to the document in saying that its conclusions are -- necessarily agree with how he looks at an area that he claims himself not to be an expert in. My objection is one of relevancy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is another issue. That is another issue, and it will be taken into consideration later on when we evaluate the various bits and pieces of the expert witness. But this is -- what I'm saying is something completely different. I mean, I don't think that your intention is to pass through the window what you cannot pass through the door, you know. I mean, it's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in relation to this report, there was a number of other questions that I wish to ask in order to expand. However, the expert witness himself, having expressed certain reservations on his own competence in this field, I wish to proceed no further. Therefore, I would like to have the specific section of the report, the one that has been discussed, admitted as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's page 93.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which means page 93 specifically, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, that is -- I have no problems with that. Judge Eser, do you have any problems? Judge Brydensholt, no? Yes, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to do two things. The first is just to underline that while I say I've done no primary research and have specific expertise on this kind of material in this area, I did suggest that I do believe myself to have a degree of authority and expertise on some of the issues associated with propaganda and use of the media in security terms, and I've been doing very specific work and research on that. But just not relating to the former Yugoslavia, although I'm aware of some -- the inferences that would be drawn from work like this. I would also point out that I do have specific knowledge of certain kinds, and if this page is being entered rather than the document, we can also note that footnote 234 on this page mentions Dusan Mitevic, who was head of the RTS, the Radio-Television Serbia, described here as an eye-opener of Milosevic, and there is evidence significantly of the way in which he specifically worked to a Milosevic agenda in deciding which things to select for broadcast and which not, and how to manage that. So the intention was certainly there within RTS, and if we'd prepared this in a different way, I could bring different examples, video extracts and examples, to go with that. So there is clear evidence that that was the intention. But I think have to be very careful when making the distinction between intention broadcast on one side and reception on the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For purposes of this part of the discussion, what I suggest is that the following pages from this report be entered into evidence, be admitted into evidence, and that's the first page of the report, and then pages 93 and 94, these two being the two pages that reference was made to during the testimony. And that would become Defence document D71. Yes, and I'm returning back ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this may be a convenient time to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree. So we'll have a 25-minute break, starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, you mentioned the UN embargo on arms of the former Yugoslavia yesterday, and you said that the Serbs found themselves at a great advantage, in fact. Is it not true that the UN embargo on the arms of the former Yugoslavia contributed significantly to bringing the Bosnian Muslims into a situation which was highly unfavourable compared to that of the Bosnian Serbs?
Yesterday I said it cemented the imbalance, to a large extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the other hand, you said that the Serbian forces that were armed and prepared for the war continued receiving significant military aid from Belgrade after the outbreak of hostilities.

I said specifically that -- not that they continued -- I would not say that they continued to receive military aid. That, to me, would be a very different proposition. That the United Kingdom might give military aid to Kuwait, that's a very different proposition from what I was saying, which was that they continued to operate as part of one integrated operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this not particularly felt in the border areas with Serbia, specifically in Podrinje, in the Drina valley, where the following towns lie: Zvornik, Bratunac, Srebrenica, in view of their proximity to Serbia?

I think we can say that the proximity of those places, and others, we could also say the same for northeastern Bosnia through to the Posavina Corridor, meant that where those instances where I make reference to forces of the VJ, those designated as VJ coming onto the territory of Bosnia-Hercegovina tended to be in eastern and northeastern Bosnia because the proximity across the border made it easier for that to happen. It being far harder, but not impossible, to get those forces across to northwestern Bosnia, and indeed sometimes forces did go to northwestern Bosnia. There was one air operation in 1994 that took pilots from Podgorica in Montenegro to the Republika Srpska Krajina where they -- where the planes were, and then they flew action for the VRS in Bosnia, again, parts of this integrated whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. Yesterday you stated that it was true that even prior to the outbreak of hostilities in Eastern Bosnia, the Serbs had heavy weaponry, including tanks, heavy artillery, even some aviation and an adequate military structure as well. Is it not true that this particular military structure made it possible for the Serbs to ethnically cleanse, in only the first two months of the war, a large number of the territories that they controlled of the non-Serb population, including the towns of Zvornik, Bratunac, and Vlasenica?
If I've got all of that together, yes. Again, that's consistent with what I was saying most of the time yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you confirm that ethnic cleansing that you spoke of yesterday was carried out on the basis of the same principle? And I'm referring particularly to the ethnic cleansing of Eastern Bosnia and the towns I mentioned, but in general, referring also to the ethnic cleansing carried out by the Serbs.
I'm sorry, could you clarify what you mean by "the same principle," please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there the same pattern of ethnic cleansing?
In that case, yes, the same pattern was used throughout the territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you briefly explain what it was that actually took place?
Do you mean can I describe events, or do you mean can I summarise what the outcome was? Or I can do both. Maybe if I do both. The outcome was that territories --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, if you may, could you explain the pattern itself.

The pattern. The elements of the pattern involved preparation, about which we've said quite a bit. They involve the preparation politically and militarily for takeover. They involve acts of provocation, usually coming from somewhere within the other town, which is -- becomes the pretext, then, for military action. The -- they involve, then, the sorting and designation of people -- of non-Serbs and non-desirables within the community, some of which would then be removed to detention centres, some of which would be processed to be evacuated, some of which would -- were, or, by that stage, might already have been killed, or in some other cases, were, then, at a later stage, killed. This is the so-called ethnic cleansing, which means removing those of a different ethnicity to ensure that there is an ethnically pure and secure, controllable framework in that particular area. The killing -- in some cases, there was demonstrative killing to induce others to cooperate in the whole process. In some cases, there appears to have been larger-scale killing. In other cases, it's been a matter more or less purely of democratic processing, either through temporary detention centres or, in some cases, even through organised arrangements to transport out. So that would include documentation, pieces of paper being signed, money being transferred to pay for a one-way ticket, to pay for a one-way visa, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. In relation to this, you stated yesterday that this principle of ethnic cleansing applied --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I need to interrupt. I'm sorry, the transcriber's asked Dr. Gow to please move closer to the microphone because she's unable to pick up all of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Forgive me. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you can move the microphones.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you were talking about ethnic cleansing yesterday, you stated that the principle of ethnic cleansing was applied by the Serb authorities and forces, and you went on to say that the same was later on copied by others. Could you please explain in more detail to the Chamber what it was that you meant by the latter part.

I think it's, by now, fairly well accepted that Croatian forces and those operating on behalf of the Bosnian government at times also practiced some similar pattern of activity, and indeed the Bosnian authorities, in some cases relating to northwest of Sarajevo, have taken responsibility themselves and have investigated and launched cases because of what was said there to have happened. So I think what I was indicating was that the incidents of atrocity and the removal of populations, while the key part of the Serbian strategy which was the core of defining the war and essentially stop -- bringing on hostilities to the region, wasn't used exclusively by those Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, this is my following question: Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether the Bosnian Muslims from Visegrad, Srebrenica, Bratunac, Zvornik carried out an ethnic cleansing of the Serbs in 1992 and in the beginning of 1993, or were they themselves victims of such an ethnic cleansing?

First, I'd wish to caution, again, about levels of expertise. My expertise principally lies with what I've referred to before as the strategic level, that military/political access overall. That means at times I have awareness also of the technical -- tactical level. That's part of building up the overall picture. I want to make clear that I don't come here as somebody with expertise on Srebrenica, or indeed Visegrad specifically and locally, at that tactical level. However, I can say that the evidence is fairly clear that Serbian campaigns of ethnic cleansing were implemented in those places, and I can also say, and this relates perhaps to the press cuttings that you showed to us before, that there were significant reports that those acting on behalf of the Bosnian government, or the Muslims, had been responsible for what were described as acts of atrocity in those parts. Now, I say this based on the evidence used by others in the reports, not because it's something that I specifically have been to that region to investigate, or have ever looked into in a very close and specific way. I point out, if you wish to have expertise on this, I have a colleague who did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was not referring to the war crimes. What I had in mind was the ethnic cleansing policy that was applied.

In that case, I should say it's probably better for me to reserve judgement that there were accusations of people being killed and removed from the territory. That is what I can say. Whether or not we should or would call that as ethnic cleansing as part of the strategy at this stage, I think, would be stretching what I can say about this situation a little bit too far.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you, Dr. Gow. Could you look once more at the map of Eastern Bosnia that we gave to you earlier on. In your -- yesterday's testimony, you said that the first attacks were a part a coordinated Serb JNA programme, designed in order to establish a control framework to all the strategic points within Bosnia and Herzegovina and outside. When talking specifically about Podrinje, the Drina area, did that also imply the takeover of the bridges leading across to Serbia?

Yes, it did. And if I may interrupt that just for a second to go back to the previous answer, it occurs to me it might be relevant also to add that while I said the Bosnian authorities have investigated some cases, I'm not aware they have investigated cases in this part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't say for sure that they haven't, but I just -- that -- an additional bit to the previous answer. On this question, yes, absolutely, the point was that those key, main communication lines into Bosnia-Herzegovina, including obviously bridges, were to be secured. Zvornik was one of those points; Visegrad was another.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it not true that in these towns of Zvornik, Visegrad, Bratunac, Vlasenica, a terrible atrocity was committed over the Bosnian Muslim population, such as killing, rape, torching, looting, expulsions, which caused a flood of refugees leaving the area?
Yes, I think that's fairly well established, and also consistent with the evidence I was giving yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it not true that an enormous number of refugees flocked to the Srebrenica area, especially at this point in time?
Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony, you also mentioned Vlasenica. Is it not true that Vlasenica was a significant place, having been placed on the main logistics route between Serbia and the units that held Sarajevo under siege at that time?
Yes, I should say that's the case, and also key in getting access over land to Han Pijesak as well, the command and control centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow, for your additional explanation. I will now show you a video featuring a part of the speech of the commander of the Drina Corps, General Milenko Zivanovic, on the establishment of the Bratunac Brigade, on the 14th of November, 1992, and it has to do with the line of questioning so far and the questions that will follow. Could you please now look at this video clip, and I kindly ask the video booth to show video 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we've seen enough. Thanks to the video booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is off. The interpreter cannot hear.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, you've said a moment ago that people were expelled. Is it not true that some of those people arrived in Srebrenica from the Vlasenica area, meaning from the north, from Vlasenica, from Bratunac, from Drina, from Skelani, therefore, from the south, thereby creating an enormous number of refugees in Srebrenica, Cerska, and in particularly in Zepce and Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed one town.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this not confirmed by this speech by General Milanovic -- Zivanovic? General Zivanovic, commander of the Drina Corps?

Where he makes reference a 80.000 Turks, I think we can take it that that means 80.000 Slav Muslims from the area, whether or not the figure is accurate. I suspect from UN figures this figure was actually less than that. But it was still tens of thousands. And yes, it confirms that that was happening, and the film also confirms, going back to one of the maps yesterday and your colleague's sound questioning of it, in line with my comment, that the three places, Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde, were not linked. And that was a key conclusion in terms of the Drina Corps commander, General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Dr. Gow. This speech by the commander of the Drina Corps that we've just listened to in the video, does it not show that the Serb army had very well worked out strategy to isolate, wear out, and cause hunger amongst the Bosnian Muslim population in the area?

Consistent with many of the other things that I've already said, it indicates that there was an approach which -- which -- which meant isolating and surrounding places, leaving them cut off, and eventually moving in to mop them up when the opportunity was there. I think we can also point out that at this stage, I don't think that significant forces from the VRS were deployed in this area precisely because it was held in one position, with no immediately significant targets, and the main emphasis was elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Before I move on to my next question, could this video clip be assigned a number, as a Defence exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We Have seen it before this video. So I would imagine that it has already been assigned a number, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Your Honour, if I may explain, we saw it as part of our opening statement, but not during the presentation of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's okay. So this video will be assigned -- is admitted into evidence, and it's being given 72.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D72.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I have no objection to the video. I just like would my learned friends to clarify what was the date of the video, when was it taken, and what does it refer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which is D71, registrar? Okay, all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This footage was made -- the video that was forwarded to us by the OTP bears the number V000-3937, and the date is the 14th of November, 1992. The establishment of the Bratunac Brigade, that was the occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, you were asked by my colleagues from the OTP yesterday about a decision to establish the army corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and your attention was drawn to the fact that Srebrenica fell under the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps, or, rather, was part of the 2nd Corps. Is it not true, then, in actual fact, that Srebrenica, as well as the two other small enclaves, Cerska and Konjevic Polje, was entirely cut off from the headquarters of the 2nd Corps, based in Tuzla?

It's certainly the case that it was physically separated, and I would also say that it was the case of an evolving situation. To say that was completely cut off, I think, would be wrong, because there were communications, including some people crossing Serbian-controlled territory to go between them throughout the whole of the period. And that includes the kind of awful moment in 1995 when the events of which we all know at Srebrenica occurred, that those in command in the area, including the defendant, had been withdrawn for a meeting just prior to those events, so that there was no -- yeah, it was physically cut off. It was not in an easy situation. But to say that there was no communication at all, I think, no -- is cut off entirely in every sense, wouldn't be accurate. If that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you, Dr. Gow. I will now show you a document. It's a Defence exhibit, D4. This is a document by the Serbian municipality of Bratunac Crisis Staff, dated the 16th of April, 1992, signed by Mr. Miroslav Deronjic. This is an order for general mobilisation.
