If you could please have a closer look -- if you could please look at the first paragraph, it reads: "Pursuant to a decision of the Presidency of the Assembly of the Republic of the Serbian People, the Crisis Staff is hereby promulgating general mobilisation for all adults. Therefore, a decision of the Assembly of the Serbian People Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality proclaiming general mobilisation in relation to all adults." Can you please just comment on the substance of this document. Is it not correct that this order for mobilisation has no age limit indicated? Would that not mean that even elderly people could have been mobilised, as well as women, in this specific case? Is that not what it seems to imply?

It has no age limit, if you mean that there's no upper age limit. It does say "who have come of age," so presumably we're talking about those of 18 or above. But there's certainly no upper limit, and the implication would be that -- or could be that certain -- that all citizens over that age, no matter who they were or which gender, could be mobilised. Whether or not citizens would also include those of Slav Muslim ethnicity as well, I don't know. But, again, theoretically, I suppose could be.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance, please. I would like to show the witness Defence Exhibit D20. This is a document from Bratunac municipality, the Birac SAO, Bratunac municipality, dated the 21st of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a list of women who are due salaries for the month of August 1992. Can you please have a look. Dr. Gow, it appears that there were women's platoons in the Serb army. Are you aware of the fact that women, too, were being mobilised at the time to join Serb units?

I'm not aware that women were being mobilised at that time. And I have to say that I can't be sure that what we're looking at here -- it's a municipality document about paying the named women on the list. It doesn't indicate at all what they're to be paid for, so I'm not sure whether or not this is linked to the idea of being mobilised or not. But I'm a little bit at a loss.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, if you could please just look carefully at this document, and there is a page with names, women, and next to the first name on the next page, it says "Platoon Commander," and next to the second name on the list, it says "Deputy Commander."
That certainly indicates -- I presume that we can assume that the abbreviation "Komanda voda" would be consistent, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. The following document may be of assistance to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe we have already had a number assigned to this document. Therefore, can we now please show the witness a document of the garrison command, Zvornik, a list of officers. This is a new document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it pleases Your Honour, could I add something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Where it says "Komanda voda" assuming that does mean commander of the platoon -- the commander of the platoon to hold the rank of lieutenant, which isn't designated. And I don't know if that has any bearing. Otherwise, it's not clear that it would necessarily have a military connotation. Maybe there could be some other way of understanding the use of "voda" as a group working. But that's a reflection on that. Are we finished with this one?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, we have. Thank you very much, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the next document now. Garrison command, Zvornik, and its name is: "List of senior officers and soldiers engaged in the sniper division in the month of October 1992." Can you now please look at the names under the numbers 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10.
So not 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Number 2 is Bogdan. No, I didn't mean him.
Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Between 3 and 10, please.

Okay. Can I also point out for the record, that the translation said "senior officers," though it says on here, but the word "officer," it only says "officer" on the original. Not that it will make a big difference, but I think accuracy ... Thanks. Sorry, Madam Vidovic, your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree, Madam Vidovic, do you agree that the inclusion of the word "senior" in the English translation is out of place, that it does not reflect the original, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do agree, Your Honours. Indeed, I do. "Starjesina" is just an officer. The word we use is "Starjesina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In relation to this question, it appears that the document contains the names of eight women who were paid salaries for that month, and we are speaking about Zvornik now. Do you have any knowledge of this; namely, that the women living in the Podrinje area were mobilised and were, in fact, actively involved in a number of different military units? Can you shed any light on this document?

I can confirm that the document has the list of female names, that it indicates them as being ordinary -- of having -- of ranking -- of being ordinary ranking soldiers, and that it indicates that they are all snipers as well, in the translation. I think what I can shed light on beyond that is that, at face value, that's what it appears to confirm. And again, in answer to the previous question, when you said at that time, I can't confirm anything I know about mobilisation of women in these areas at that time. This would appear to confirm it; that women were mobilised, I don't think that anybody would dispute, and that that's part of a tradition in the region, certainly going back to the Second World War, of women being mobilised and taking part in the military activity, as relevant. Does that ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please assign a number to this document before I move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document is being tendered and admitted in evidence and marked as Defence document D73. Yes, Judge Eser would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic, in this document there's a column called employment, organisation, probably, or institution, but there's nothing marked, is there? Now, if you take the front line, you have here the rank, duty, place of residence, and then employment, organisation, probably, or institution, and there's nothing listed here as an explanation for this empty place. Or could the expert give an interpretation for this?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the expert has indicated, but I might as well answer your question, Your Honour. The place of residence, as indicated, si where those women actually resided. As for the empty boxes under employment, organisation or institution, what this means is that they were not in their usual jobs but rather had received a war assignment, as indicated by this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, I would like to draw your attention to something else. I believe the expert witness has the document in front of him. He can see the following, columns 2, drafted in the unit from -- you do agree, Dr. Gow, in case you still have the document before you, that's indeed what it states, drafted in the unit from the 1st of September to the 17th of September, and the number of days that they spent working as --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: October.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: -- and the number of days working as snipers, from, to, the dates of engagement.

If you're asking me to confirm that those dates are on the document, I can do that. I was about to point that out, that these engagements were for limited periods, amounting to no more than 17 days on this basis here. I was going to seek to assist Your Honour in terms of the empty column. I suspect that because it's -- this document relates to a draft, that column, and this is only -- it's a form of speculation, trying to interpret the empty column, would refer to the institution in which the drafted person was based or the place of employment, but I suspect that in this situation at that time, in these contexts, either they had no employment to register or it was unknown, would be the most likely explanation of the empty column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe this would be a convenient place to break my cross-examination. If not, I have another document to show, but that may take a little time, and I'd prefer to do it tomorrow, if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might take the floor just for a moment, since Madam Vidovic has stopped her cross-examination at this point. The Prosecution would like to note that, in our opinion, the cross-examination of our expert witness, Dr. Gow, appears to be more of an eliciting of evidence that certainly doesn't contradict anything that's in Dr. Gow's statement. I do understand that in the very beginning, our learned friend did say that she would like to clarify some things, but I think we have reached the point, after the two sessions of cross-examination, where we have either clarified, but we certainly are not cross-examining. The Prosecution would like to renew its request of the Defence, according to their eliciting of this evidence, to stipulate to certain facts that we've asked them to stipulate for -- in prior correspondence. And I would just like to note our correspondence included in the pre-trial brief of the 30th of September, we asked them to stipulate to certain things, and among the issues they at that time period did not stipulate to was that, at all times relevant to this indictment, the indictment against Mr. Oric, a state of international armed conflict existed on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We are under the distinct impression today that they certainly seem to support that evidence that we elicited, and that they clarified through elicitation. We would like to know at this point, would they stipulate. Another fact that they informed us that they could not stipulate to that pertains to the indictment against Mr. Oric is, with the disintegration of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, a cadre staff consisting of former JNA officers began to prepare the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it appears to me today that their evidence supports it, elicits possibly even more evidence on it. And then I would say the last fact that they indicated to us they would not be able to stipulate to at that time, but it seems today that they do stipulate to, that the JNA provided critical combat, financial, and logistical support to military organisations carried out by the VRS against the non-Serb population in Bosnia-Herzegovina. These are part of our general allegations. We would like to renew our request to have the Defence stipulate as opposed to continuing to elicit this evidence. And then lastly, I might add, Your Honours, that possibly in the interests of judicial economy, while we are quite pleased with the presence of Dr. Gow, I'm certain our learned friends are also, but if they would like to further elicit evidence on this point, then I believe that might be something that they could incorporate into the Defence case. And to use Dr. Gow's time here possibly to cross-examine him on something that they disagree with, either in his report or in his testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think this debate should not be continued in the presence of Dr. Gow, in any case, so that's the first thing. I'm going to adjourn the sitting. I would like to have -- at this point, he should not be involved in the discussion for sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the discussion, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, registrar, please, could we have this part of the debate copied for us, to have it available tomorrow morning? We'll start with these points. You will have time to think about what has been raised by Ms. Sellers and to give us your point of view tomorrow. You're not in this -- you do not come into this debate. You're there to answer questions that are put to you in direct or in cross, and don't worry about the rest, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I say something, not about this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With your indulgence. I wanted to say two things relating to the earlier part of the morning, if I may. The first is, I raised a question about the Federal Secretariat for Defence document I was shown, simply because of the different typography. While I was sitting on my own in the room in the last break, I was looking through a bundle of things that had been passed to me on Sunday night by the Prosecutor from the -- I understand from the Defence, which I had flipped then but didn't know what to make of it. I saw that document was included in there and appeared to have one of these ERN numbers on it already. So I assume from that that it's been admitted and used somewhere else, and I just want to note that I -- that that was in that bundle. I have seen that in a version which has an ERN on it. And another thing, if you permit me 30 seconds more, goes back to the media propaganda question. I think it's also important to understand in that context that those who are successful with propaganda, with information for a particular intent and purpose, do so by understanding the audience. And there are things called tropes or particularly images and ideas. So the more you use those and reinforce them, the more likely you are to be to mobilise the support. And I think that's important to understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. Thank you, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will return tomorrow morning to continue and finish with your cross-examination, tomorrow morning at 9.00, okay? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, 24 November 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
